articles.title: Your Demo Server Should Never Hold the Model Key
articles.excerpt: A public demo needs a model, but it does not need the credential that pays for it. When free model access and a free server option push the cost of shipping a demo close to zero, the cheapest possible…
articles.body: A public demo needs a model, but it does not need the credential that pays for it. When free model access and a free server option push the cost of shipping a demo close to zero, the cheapest possible architecture also becomes the riskiest one: paste the provider key into the host's environment variables, forget about it, and hope nobody looks. I want to walk you through a different arrangement, where the key lives in one small process you control and the public server only ever holds a token that expires. MonkeyCode advertises free model access and a free server option, which is precisely the kind of offer that makes pasting a key into a demo tempting on a Friday afternoon. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.
articles.author: Riley Lin

articles.title: Two Free Adapters, One Contract to Test
articles.excerpt: Two Free Adapters, One Contract to Test A free tier is a contract, not a promise. Write the contract down first. Then test it before you build on it. Most teams do this backwards. They wire the free e…
articles.body: Two Free Adapters, One Contract to Test A free tier is a contract, not a promise. Write the contract down first. Then test it before you build on it. Most teams do this backwards. They wire the free endpoint into the app, ship, and learn the rules when something breaks. That is not architecture review. That is archaeology after the outage. This is an architecture review you can run this week. Two ports, two adapters, one contract suite. The free model and the free server stay replaceable. Name the constraints before you name the vendor Start with a constraint interview. Write the answers down. Where you have no answer, write unknown . Ask three things of every free dependency. What is the capacity, and who counts it? What happens at the boundary — error, silence, or throttle?

articles.excerpt: Originally published at GeekCoding101. On October 31 the DeepSeek Harness team pushed a single commit to deepseek-ai/dsh-superagent-prototype and the repository went past 9,000 stars in under two days…
articles.body: Originally published at GeekCoding101 . Why Everyone Is Talking About It On October 31 the DeepSeek Harness team pushed a single commit to deepseek-ai/dsh-superagent-prototype and the repository went past 9,000 stars in under two days. It's a proactive coding agent for one GitHub repository : it watches the repo (and optionally Feishu chats), decides on its own which messages are real requests for work, opens a work item for each, runs it in its own agent session and directory, and answers in the original conversation, usually with a pull request. Every write-up I found is a paraphrase of the README: "router-worker architecture", "saves human attention", "p95 15.7 minutes vs 29.5". Not one of them installed it. So I did.

articles.title: Opinion: Your Agent's Lock-In Is the Tool Schema, Not the Model
articles.excerpt: Model swaps are cheap now. Tool schema swaps are not. That asymmetry is where your lock-in actually lives. Everyone benchmarks the model. Almost nobody benchmarks the tool contract. I think that gap i…
articles.body: Model swaps are cheap now. Tool schema swaps are not. That asymmetry is where your lock-in actually lives. Everyone benchmarks the model. Almost nobody benchmarks the tool contract. I think that gap is the most expensive blind spot in agent work right now. The model swaps in an afternoon Wrapping a new endpoint takes one adapter file. You change a base URL and a model id. Your prompts survive. Your eval set survives. Tool calling is different. Every endpoint has opinions about argument shape. Some honor additionalProperties: false . Some quietly ignore it. Some invent a third call you never declared. Those differences do not show up in a chat transcript. They show up as a 400 from your executor at 2am. Or worse, a silent write to the wrong path.

articles.title: robots.txt Redirects: Keep the Rules Attached to the Original Host
articles.excerpt: When a robots.txt request redirects to another host, trace the complete HTTP route and evaluate the returned rules in the context of the original request. The location holding the policy file and the…
articles.body: When a robots.txt request redirects to another host, trace the complete HTTP route and evaluate the returned rules in the context of the original request. The location holding the policy file and the site governed by that request are different facts. Keep both in your evidence before deciding whether a public documentation page is allowed to be crawled. A redirect can be intentional, such as a shared policy service. It can also be an accidental consequence of a hostname or application routing change. The useful engineering task is to identify which file the crawler can reach and what that file means for the initial site. A successful browser visit to some policy text is only the beginning of that check.

articles.title: Ongoing Website Maintenance: A Practical Checklist by Cadence
articles.excerpt: Most sites don't fail on launch day. They fail months later, when updates pile up, backups were never tested, and a contact form quietly stops working. Here's a simple routine: Daily/automated: availa…
articles.body: Most sites don't fail on launch day. They fail months later, when updates pile up, backups were never tested, and a contact form quietly stops working. Here's a simple routine: Daily/automated: availability alerts, backup status, critical transaction failures Weekly: test key forms and visitor journeys, review pending updates Monthly: content accuracy, performance trends, search reports, access changes Quarterly: restore test, supplier scope review, broader usability review A few rules that make it work: Give every task an owner and a definition of "done". "Check contact form" means submit a test inquiry and confirm delivery. Back up before every major update, and test the restore, not just the backup.

articles.title: One line of JSON stops the pump
articles.excerpt: How I gave a Claude Code agent ears, a seat in the plant's Discord, and a supervisor to answer to. Built for the Flip the Switch hackathon. A pump tells you it is failing weeks before it fails. It hum…
articles.body: How I gave a Claude Code agent ears, a seat in the plant's Discord, and a supervisor to answer to. Built for the Flip the Switch hackathon. A pump tells you it is failing weeks before it fails. It hums at a new pitch. A bearing starts to hiss. An impeller picks up a fresh tone. The fitter who walks past it every morning sometimes hears it. Usually the plant hears it when the pump stops. Across Southern Africa, mills, mines, cold rooms, and borehole pumps run on ear and experience. Vibration sensors cost more than the pump. Every fitter already carries a phone. The brief for Flip the Switch was simple: let the machine speak in the chat the team already uses, and keep every decision about the machine with a person.

articles.title: Giant exoplanet emerges from the dark when the James Webb Space Telescope turns out the starlight
articles.excerpt: Astronomers have filtered out starlight from James Webb Space Telescope observations to see a giant exoplanet emerge in the darkness.
articles.body: Sometimes science can seem really counter-intuitive. For example, occasionally in astronomy, you can see more with less light. Case in point: the emergence of a giant planet in observations made by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), when astronomers found a way to block out light from the planet's parent star. The extrasolar planet, or exoplanet , in question is 51 Eridani b (51 ERI b), a gas giant with the same mass as around 11 Jupiters that orbits a star located around 97 light-years away. 51 ERI b was discovered back in 2015 by ground-based telescopes, but the planet was missing from observations of the system made by the JWST.

articles.body: The Didymos binary asteroid system, as seen by Europe's Hera probe. The main asteroid, Didymos, dominates the frame while just a sliver of its "moonlet," Dimorphos, is visible beneath it. ESA released this image on Nov. 5, 2026. (Image credit: ESA) The European Space Agency 's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has gotten its first close-up look at the Didymos binary asteroid system. If that system sounds familiar, it's because it made headlines in September 2022 when NASA's DART (Double Asteroid Redirection Test) spacecraft smashed into it. The aim of the DART mission was to test whether an impact could divert an asteroid away from a collision course with Earth. The purpose of Hera is to follow up on DART by making up-close observations of the Didymos system.

articles.title: Northern lights could reach New York and Idaho this weekend as speedy solar wind races toward Earth
articles.excerpt: A colossal coronal hole on the sun is unleashing a stream of high-speed solar wind that could spark impressive auroras Nov. 6-8.
articles.body: The northern lights could put on an impressive display this weekend as a colossal coronal hole on the sun fires a stream of high-speed solar wind toward Earth. Minor (G1) geomagnetic storm conditions between Nov. 6 and Nov. 8, with a chance of moderate (G2) conditions on Nov. 7 and Nov. 8, according to NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) . If G2 conditions materialize, the northern lights could be visible as far south as New York and Idaho. What is happening? The culprit behind the potential uptick in northern lights is a large coronal hole on the sun , a region where the sun's magnetic field opens up. They allow streams of charged particles known as the solar wind to escape more easily into space.

articles.title: Max Power: NASA hosting its 1st air show this weekend on Florida's Space Coast
articles.excerpt: NASA will host a first-of-its-kind air show and aerospace expo on Florida's Space Coast this weekend —an event that shares its name with one of Homer Simpson's aliases.
articles.body: NASA will host a first-of-its-kind air show and aerospace expo on Florida's Space Coast this weekend. The show, called Max Power, will take place Saturday and Sunday (Nov. 7 and Nov. 8) at and around NASA's Kennedy Space Center (KSC). That name should be familiar to "Simpsons" fans, by the way: Max Power is an alias that Homer uses in the 13th episode of the show's 10th season. (He got it off a hair dryer.)
